source.title: Progressive Behavioral Drift through Compression Valleys in Large Language Models
source.authors: Zhiyuan Xu; Stanislav Abaimov; Joseph Gardiner; Sana Belguith

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some table and figure formatting is flattened, but the relevant Evil scores in Tables 2, 7, and 8 are attributable to their conditions.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses attention sinks and compression valleys as the basis for an activation-space attack, then reports how its own steering method performs. It does not test the listed fine-tuning, KL-position, compliant-prefill, suffix/decoding-bypass, weight-localization, shallowness-cause, or deepening claims.
record.gate_note: The paper does not fine-tune models on harmful or benign examples, measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, prefill compliant response tokens, test adversarial suffixes, localize safety in weights, or train deeper safety. Its Evil evaluation uses deliberately induced activation steering on prompts designed to elicit malicious or unethical tendencies indirectly; those results are recorded as related findings under versions ["none"], not as evidence of harmful-request compliance or ordinary safety behavior. Layer-selection scores are used to select layers, so they are not included. The study also reports guardrail detection rates, but those measure detector performance rather than the model behavior named in the claim.
record.test_reason: The study proposes an inference-time activation-steering attack (SSS) built on attention sinks and compression valleys. It measures how far its own method shifts targeted behaviours. It does no harmful or benign fine-tuning, no per-token KL between aligned and base models, no prefilling, suffix or decoding attack on refusal, no weight localization, and no deepening training. Its Evil results come from deliberately induced steering on indirect persona prompts, not harmful-request compliance. The shallow-safety paper (Qi et al. 2024) is cited only in the ethics appendix. The method does not rely on shallow alignment, so T6/cites_only fits better than the reader's T4/uses_without_test.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that attention sinks and compression valleys form high-gain regions. They find BOS-anchored, sensitivity-scaled perturbations produce progressive behavioural drift with little coherence or MMLU/GSM8K loss. They note the effect is limited for short generations and early refusals in heavily aligned models. They argue safety analysis should monitor internal trajectories.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses inference-time activation-space steering, not harmful or benign fine-tuning, per-token KL measurement, compliant-prefix prefilling, or safety-depth training. It compares its activation method with ActAdd and CAA.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported effects vary by model and targeted behavior; Evil steering is especially limited for short generations and early refusals. The paper also evaluates different decoding temperatures, selected layers, and steering schedules.

fits_no_version.finding: SSS raises judged Evil scores over benign baselines on all four models, but only weakly on GPT-OSS-20B (8.7 vs 0.0, below CAA's 26.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-space steering can induce indirect malicious-tendency outputs in instruction-tuned models, with strength depending on model and alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: SSS Evil scores stay above benign at T=0.6 and T=1.0 for Qwen3-14B and Llama-3.1-8B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SSS-induced Evil scores persist under stochastic decoding for the two models tested.

fits_no_version.finding: Pooled SSS Evil score rises from 18.6 (short) to 33.7 (medium) to 69.4 (long). The authors say short completions typically correspond to early refusals.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early-terminating refusals limit progressive activation steering; harmful drift emerges mainly in long generations.

fits_no_version.finding: On 231 high-scoring Qwen3-14B Evil generations, Llama-Guard-3-8B flags 60.1% and Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B flags 74.5% as harmful. This is detector performance, not a model behaviour rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Output guardrails miss a sizeable share of harm spread over long, gradually drifting generations.

record.problems: The Evil prompts are indirect and the behavior is deliberately induced, so these results do not directly establish harmful-request compliance or ordinary safety failure. Behavior scores rely primarily on an LLM judge, although the paper reports human and additional-judge checks for Beshift rather than Evil. No confidence intervals or error bars are stated for the extracted Evil scores. The paper itself notes that effectiveness depends on generation length and that short refusals constrain the attack.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version rows were eligible. Evil-axis rows for SSS and its reported comparison methods, stochastic settings, and length bins are retained because they measure the related induced behavior. Other behavior axes, coherence scores, detector performance, and general-capability scores were left out as they do not measure the claim's named safety behavior.

untested.parts: No harmful-example fine-tuning; no harmful-request compliance rate.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL. Directional projection onto steering vectors is a different measure.
No compliant-prefix prefilling, adversarial suffixes or decoding-change attacks on refusal. Activation steering is outside this version's named methods.
No weight or rank localization of safety. Layer selection concerns steering efficacy, not safety parameters.
No analysis of whether data or training objectives cause shallow safety.
No safety-deepening training or its robustness.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from uses_without_test/T4 to cites_only/T6. The study cites Qi et al. 2024 only in the ethics appendix and does not use shallow alignment as a tool. Its passing remark that early benign tokens evade first-token-based filters is conceptually adjacent to V4 but is not a test. Evil prompts are indirect persona questions with a prompt suffix requesting long answers, which inflates generation length. Scores come from a Gemini-2.5-Flash judge with no uncertainty reported; cross-judge and human checks cover Beshift only.

versions.untested_parts: Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Compliant-prefix prefilling, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes as ways to bypass refusal.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety shallowness.
Training that deepens safety and whether such training is robust.
